title: MA9-00819
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant is XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Mexico, who claims refugee status pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the Act).

During the month of XXXX 2006, the claimant opened a family business XXXX XXXX, referred to as a "XXXX", in the municipality of XXXX, in the State of Vera Cruz. Thereafter, he formed an association with his friend, XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX), who was a pig farmer. The claimant would give XXXX the prunnings, that is the husks and cobs from the corn, in order to feed his pigs, and in return, he would receive from XXXX several animals.

During a holiday celebration on XXXX XXXX, 2007, XXXX received a call that there was a problem at his farm and that he should return home. The claimant decided to go with him. Upon arrival, they were beaten by several men who stated that they belonged to a criminal organization and that it would be better for the claimant and XXXX to cooperate with them. The criminals demanded that the claimant and XXXX pay them for protection each month the sum of 3,000 pesos, and threatened their lives and those of their families if they were to file a complaint with the police. Both the claimant and XXXX paid their share of the 3,000 pesos every month, even though it was becoming more difficult to raise the money. On XXXX XXXX, 2008, the claimant was advised that his friend XXXX was wounded and had been shot in the throat and required a blood transfusion. The claimant feared for the lives of the members of his family and decided to move to a ranch in the municipality of XXXX XXXX, a 40 minute drive outside of XXXX. Two days later, XXXX died from his wounds and at that point the claimant decided to flee to Canada to seek protection. He arrived at Montréal on XXXX XXXX, 2008, and filed for refugee protection upon his arrival.
The Tribunal finds that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" as contemplated by section 96, and is not a "person in need of protection" as set forth in section 97(1) of the Act.
The identity of the claimant has been established on the basis of a genuine Mexican passport.

The Tribunal finds that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee", as his fear of persecution is not by reason of any of the five grounds set out in section 96 of the Act. Moreover, the Tribunal determines that he is not a "person in need of protection", as set forth in section 97(1) of the Act, since the evidence presented in support of his allegations does not establish the likelihood, on a balance of probabilities, of a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if he were to return to Mexico.

The Tribunal finds that there is a lack of credibility with respect to determinative issues. Furthermore, the Tribunal finds that the claimant has not rebutted the presumption that Mexico is capable of protecting its citizens, and in addition, the Tribunal is of the opinion that internal flight alternatives exist for the claimant.

There are contradictions and inconsistencies in the claimant's evidence. On January 21, 2009, he completed a form "Annexe 1- Renseignements de Base",1 and in response to question 7, he stated that he worked as an employee in the family business from the month of October 2006 until August 2008; whereas in his Personal Information Form (PIF)2 in response to question 31, he states that he moved with his family outside of XXXX on XXXX XXXX, 2008. In response to question 7 of Annexe 1, where he was required to provide precise information for every location for every month where he lived during the past ten years, he states that he lived in XXXX until the month of August 2008, and makes no reference to having moved to the municipality of XXXX XXXX during the month of July 2008. The Tribunal concludes that the claimant, until his departure for Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2008, never left the municipality of XXXX.

At his hearing, the claimant testified that at the end of each month, a member of the criminal gang would come to his "XXXX" to collect 1,500 pesos, and that the last payment he made was at the end of the month of XXXX 2008. He stated that he had prepared the money for the payment at the end of June; however, no one came to collect it. At paragraph 11 of his response to question 31 of the PIF, he states that he did not make the payment due at the end of the month of June 2008, because he did not have enough money. When asked at his hearing to explain the apparent inconsistency, he was unable to do so.

At his hearing, the claimant testified that he and XXXX would speak by telephone one time per week, and because of their fear of being overheard, they would speak in code. The last time they spoke during the month of July 2008, the claimant told XXXX that his payment for the month of June had not been collected; whereas XXXX indicated to the claimant that he had made his own payment. The Tribunal asked the claimant if he could explain why XXXX would have been shot in the throat by the criminal gang members who were extorting money if he in fact had made the payment that was due at the end of the month of June 2008. The claimant stated that at the hospital, the police told him that XXXX was shot by criminals; however, there is no evidence that the criminals that shot XXXX were in any way connected with the criminals who were extorting money from XXXX and the claimant. In other words, there is no cogent evidence to link the killing of XXXX with the gang of criminals who were forcing the claimant and XXXX to pay "protection" money.

The claimant acknowledged at his hearing that most people who operate businesses in the region where the claimant lived were forced to pay "protection" money to the criminal elements. Although the claimant testified that on some unspecified date after he left Mexico, his wife received an anonymous telephone call threatening to kidnap her son, who was at school, unless she paid a sum of money, nothing ever came of such threat, and the claimant is unable to establish that there was any connection between such threat and the threats which he received extorting money from his business. The claimant has been in Canada for almost four years and acknowledges that his family has not received any threats from the gang of criminals that extorted money from him. He states that the "XXXX" was closed when he left Mexico, and his family moved outside of XXXX, in the municipality of XXXX XXXX. In any event, it does not appear that any effort was made by the gang of criminals to locate the claimant or members of his family.

The claimant acknowledged that he never considered filing a complaint with the police because of the threats received to his life and that of members of his family. In the opinion of the Tribunal, the claimant has not discharged the burden of proving that he has taken all reasonable steps to seek state protection, and he has not demonstrated that he would have put his life in danger had he attempted to file a complaint against the gang of criminals. By making no effort to file a denunciation with the police, the Tribunal is of the opinion that the claimant has not rebutted the presumption that Mexico is capable of protecting its citizens, and concludes that state protection would have been reasonably forthcoming.

Even if the Tribunal were to determine that state protection is inadequate, which is not the case, the Tribunal is of the opinion that internal flight alternatives exist for the claimant. The claimant spent five years in the United States working in construction, and furthermore has several years of experience in Mexico XXXX XXXX. The claimant acknowledged at his hearing that in all likelihood he could find work anywhere in Mexico; however, he stated that there is violence wherever he would go in Mexico. He believes that he would have to register his location such that the criminal gang would be able to locate him. In the opinion of the Tribunal, the criminal gang has made no apparent effort to locate the claimant during the past four years, and it is not likely that the claimant's life would be in danger in any other region of Mexico, and the Tribunal concludes that it would not be objectively unreasonable to expect the claimant to move to another, less hostile part of Mexico before seeking refugee status in Canada.

The Tribunal concludes that on a balance of probabilities, there is no reasonable chance or serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted if he were to return to Mexico. In the same manner, on a balance of probabilities, more likely than not, the claimant would not be subject personally to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if he were to return to Mexico. In the opinion of the Tribunal, the risk of the claimant being a victim of extortion in order to force him to pay "protection" money as a business man, as admitted by the claimant, is a risk faced generally by other merchants in the municipality of XXXX, in the State of Vera Cruz, and would not give rise to a claim for protection under section 97(1) of the Act.

For the foregoing reasons, the Tribunal concludes that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96, or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97(1) of the Act. Edward Aronoff Me Edward Aronoff July 31, 2012 Date /cm 1 Exhibit A-2 : Immigration documents. 2 Ibid. --------------- --------------- --------------- --------------- RPD File No. / No dossier SPR : MA9-00819 6
